back: King Narmer (Menes) unified Upper and Lower Egypt and founded the first dynasty, marking the start of the Egyptian state.
extra: He established a centralized monarchy and began the tradition of pharaohs ruling both lands.

front: Drought at the end of the Middle Kingdom (c. 1786 BC)
back: A severe Nile failure and social unrest ended the Middle Kingdom and opened the Second Intermediate Period, when Hyksos rulers controlled the Delta.
extra: It showed how dependent Egyptian civilization was on the Nile's annual flood.

back: One of the few women to rule Egypt as pharaoh; she expanded trade to the Land of Punt and commissioned the temple at Deir el-Bahari.
extra: Her successors, especially Thutmose III, later tried to erase her name from royal records.

back: The most celebrated of the New Kingdom pharaohs; he built the Ramesseum, the two temples at Abu Simbel, and the Sphinx at Memphis.
extra: He fought the Hittites at the Battle of Kadesh (c. 1274 BC) and then signed the first known peace treaty.

back: Around 1200 BC the Mycenaean palaces, Ugarit, and parts of Hittite territory fell to the mysterious 'Sea Peoples' and internal disruptions.
extra: Egypt survived under Merneptah and Ramses III, which is why the Egyptians preserved the record of the events.

back: Sumer (southern Iraq) was the first urban civilization; its independent cities such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash each had a temple, a king (ensi) and a scribe class.
extra: They developed irrigation canals that turned the marshy alluvial plain into surplus agriculture.

back: The earliest writing system was invented in Sumer; scribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay tablets with reed styluses.
extra: Early tablets recorded grain, oil and beer rations; later literature such as the Epic of Gilgamesh was written in it.

back: Uruk was the largest Sumerian city; legend credits its hero-king Gilgamesh with building its walls and founding epic tradition.
extra: The Epic of Gilgamesh is the oldest surviving work of literature (c. 2100 BC in Sumerian).

back: Ziggurats were stepped temple-towers dedicated to the city's patron god; the great ziggurat of Ur was dedicated to Nanna (the moon god).
extra: They were not pyramids; they were platforms on top of which the priest's temple stood.

back: Sargon of Akkad united the Sumerian cities under one rule and founded the first true empire in history, extending from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean.
extra: He used professional armies and garrison towns to hold the empire together.

back: The Babylonian king Hammurabi issued a 282-article stone stele that is the best-known ancient law code; it covers trade, family, labour and punishment.
extra: It states 'an eye for an eye', but punishments differed by social class.

back: After the Hittites destroyed Babylon, the Kassites from the Zagros mountains ruled Babylon for over four centuries, the longest continuous dynasty in the ancient Near East.
extra: They strengthened the temples and the city walls.

back: The Assyrian kings Sargon II, Sennacherib, Ashurbanipal and others built the largest military empire of the ancient world, with capital at Nimrud, Nineveh and Dur-Sharrukin.
extra: Ashurbanipal founded the great library at Nineveh, whose clay tablets survive today in the British Museum.

back: The Neo-Babylonian king who conquered Jerusalem in 586 BC, built the Ishtar Gate, the Hanging Gardens (legendary) and the great ziggurat Etemenanki.
extra: The destruction of the First Temple is commemorated in the Book of Lamentations.

back: The Persian king Xerxes crossed the Hellespont with a huge army and navy; after the defeat of Thermopylae the Greek ships defeated the Persians at the naval Battle of Salamis.
extra: Salamis (September 480 BC) decided the course of the Greco-Persian Wars.

back: Spartan boys entered the state-run agoge at age seven; they trained in weapons, endurance, music and silence, and lived in barracks until thirty.
extra: The system produced the famous hoplite warrior-soldiers.

front: Critias and the Thirty Tyrants (404 BC)
back: At the end of the Peloponnesian War the Spartan-backed oligarchy of the Thirty Tyrants, led by Critias, ruled Athens for about eight months with terror and executions.
extra: The democratic exile Ledos (Thrasybulus) marched on Athens in 403 BC and restored the democracy.

back: Son of Philip II of Macedon, Alexander conquered the Persian Empire, Egypt, Mesopotamia and reached the Indus in ten years, dying in Babylon aged thirty-two.
extra: He founded over twenty cities named Alexandria; Alexandria in Egypt became the new intellectual capital of the Hellenic world.

back: Alexander's companion cavalry swept around the Persian king Darius III's centre at Gaugamela (near modern Erbil) and won the decisive battle that ended the Achaemenid Empire.
extra: Darius fled; the Persian capital Persepolis was sacked and burned in 330 BC.

back: After conquering Persia Alexander pushed into the Central Asian satrapies of Bactria and Sogdiana, where his mutinous troops finally refused to march further east.
extra: He married the Bactrian princess Roxana (Roxane) in 327 BC; she outlived him and claimed the throne.

back: After Alexander's death in 323 BC his general-diadochi fought over his empire; by about 300 BC three large kingdoms had emerged: the Ptolemaic, the Seleucid and the Antigonid Macedon.
extra: Their courts patronized philosophy, science and epic poetry (e.g. Callimachus in Alexandria, Aratus in Macedon).

back: The first Ptolemaic king of Egypt; he founded the city of Alexandria, the Library and the Mouseion (Museum), and promoted Greek culture in Egypt.
extra: His grandson Ptolemy II Philadelphus greatly enlarged the Library, reputedly with over 400,000 scrolls.

back: The royal collection of scrolls in Ptolemaic Alexandria, staffed by scholars such as Euclid, Eratosthenes and Aristarchus, was the great research library of the ancient world.
extra: It housed copies of nearly every Greek and Egyptian text; it was damaged and dispersed over several centuries, notably in 48 BC during Caesar's civil war.

back: Head of the Library of Alexandria; he calculated the Earth's circumference by comparing the sun's angle in Syene and Alexandria, with only a 2% error.
extra: He also invented the grid of latitude and longitude and the sieve for finding primes.

back: Octavian, victor over Mark Antony at Actium (31 BC), took the name Augustus in 27 BC and became the first Roman emperor, ending the civil wars of the Republic.
extra: He is said to have found Rome brick and left it marble; his Res Gestae narrates his reign.

back: At Actium in the Ionian Sea, Octavian's fleet under Agrippa destroyed the forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra, ending the last phase of the Roman civil wars.
extra: Cleopatra and Antony committed suicide; Octavian became the sole master of the Roman world and took the title Augustus.

back: The last Julio-Claudian emperor, Nero, is remembered for his artistic ambitions, his tyranny and for blaming Christians for the Great Fire of Rome (AD 64).
extra: His assassination in 68 AD ended the Julio-Claudian line and began the Year of the Four Emperors.

front: Constantine and the Council of Nicaea (325 AD)
back: The first Christian Roman emperor, Constantine, called the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD to settle the Arian controversy and produced the Nicene Creed.
extra: He moved the capital to Constantinople (330 AD) and granted legal toleration to all religions with the Edict of Milan (313 AD).

back: The last great emperor of the classical Roman world; his general Belisarius reconquered North Africa, Italy and parts of Spain, and Justinian issued the Corpus Juris Civilis.
extra: The plague of Justinian (541-542 AD) killed perhaps a third of the empire and ended the reconquest.

back: A bubonic plague epidemic struck Constantinople and the Mediterranean world, killing perhaps a quarter of the population of the Roman Empire and weakening the Byzantine state.
extra: It is thought to have been the first recorded pandemic of Yersinia pestis.

back: The Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II breached the Theodosian walls and captured the last Byzantine capital, ending over a thousand years of Roman-Byzantine rule.
extra: Greek scholars fled west to Italy and helped to fuel the Renaissance.

back: From a small beylik in Anatolia the Ottoman sultans took Constantinople (1453), the Balkans and Egypt (1517), and for three centuries controlled the eastern Mediterranean and the trade routes to Asia.
extra: The Ottomans were also the protectors of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina from 1517.

back: Under the Abbasid caliphate (750-1258) and earlier Umayyad and Fatimid courts, Muslim scholars in Baghdad, Cordoba, Cairo and Samarkand advanced mathematics, astronomy, medicine and chemistry far ahead of Europe.
extra: Al-Khwarizmi's book on algebra gave the word 'algebra' its name; al-Razi and Ibn Sina (Avicenna) were leading physicians of the period.

back: The Persian mathematician at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad; his book 'Kitab al-Jabr' gave the term 'algebra' and his name the term 'algorithm'.
extra: He also compiled a table of sines and improved the Indian-Arabic numeral system that Europe later adopted.

back: The Persian polymath whose 'Canon of Medicine' was the standard medical textbook in Europe and the Islamic world for six hundred years.
extra: He also wrote on philosophy, optics, alchemy and music; his name became 'Avicenna' in Latin.

back: The great Asharite theologian; his 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' argued against the rationalist philosophers and his 'Revival of the Religious Sciences' became a standard of Sufi spirituality.
extra: He spent a period of doubt and wandering before returning to scholarship; his work shaped Islamic thought for centuries.

back: The First Crusade was preached by Pope Urban II at Clermont (1095) and the crusaders captured Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, founding the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
extra: The 'People's Crusade' of Peter the Hermit was destroyed in Asia Minor before the main force arrived.

back: Saladin's recapture of Jerusalem in 1187 prompted the Third Crusade, in which Richard I of England ('the Lionheart'), Philip II of France and the German emperor Frederick Barbarossa came east.
extra: After Frederick drowned in Asia Minor and Philip went home, Richard alone negotiated a treaty with Saladin (1192) that left the Holy Land in Muslim hands but opened the coast to pilgrims.

back: The Kurdish-Ayyubid sultan who reunified Syria and Egypt, defeated the Franks at Hattin (1187) and recaptured Jerusalem, and who was famed for his chivalry even by his European enemies.
extra: He is remembered in the Song of Roland tradition and by Shakespeare as a noble king.

back: The Muslim forces of Saladin ambushed the Crusader army near the Horns of Hattin (in modern Galilee), destroyed it and took its king Guy of Lusignan prisoner.
extra: Within a year Saladin had retaken all of the Holy Land except the coastal fortress cities.

back: A military order founded after the First Crusade to guard pilgrims and hold fortresses in the Latin East; at its height it owned castles, banks and estates across Europe.
extra: In 1307 Philip IV of France had the Templars arrested on false charges and the order was formally dissolved by Pope Clement V in 1312.

back: The medieval system in which a lord granted a fief (land) in return for military service, and peasants worked the lord's demesne in exchange for protection.
extra: It arose from the collapse of central authority after the fall of the Roman Empire and was reinforced by the Christian Church.

back: A vassal swore fealty to a lord, received a fief, and owed military service, advice and help in court; the lord owed the vassal protection and justice.
extra: The chain of oaths (king, dukes, counts, knights, freemen) defined the social hierarchy.

back: The bubonic plague that killed a third to a half of Europe's population between 1347 and 1351, probably arriving from Asia via Genoese trading ships at Marseille and Novgorod.
extra: It broke down the feudal labour supply, raised wages, and contributed to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in England.

back: The English peasants rebelled under the leadership of Wat Tyler and John Ball against the poll tax and feudal dues; King Richard II met the rebels at Mile End and Smithfield.
extra: Wat Tyler was killed and the revolt was crushed, but the poll tax was withdrawn.

back: Barons forced the English king John to accept a charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing due process ('no free man shall be seized or imprisoned save by the lawful judgment of his peers') and capping feudal payments.
extra: Though quickly annulled by Pope Innocent III, it became a symbol of the rule of law and of constitutional government.

back: The longest-reigning British monarch; under her the British Empire reached its greatest extent (a quarter of the world's land and a fifth of its people) and the Industrial Revolution transformed the economy.
extra: The 'Victoria cross' and 'Victoria era' are named for her; her grandson Edward VII and great-grandson George V followed on the throne.

back: The cultural rebirth that began in the city-states of northern Italy (Florence, Venice, Milan, Rome) in the 14th century and spread across Europe, reviving interest in classical Greek and Roman art and literature.
extra: It was fuelled by the wealth of banking families such as the Medici, the fall of Constantinople (1453) that brought Greek scholars west, and the invention of the printing press.

back: The Florentine banking dynasty that bankrolled popes, kings and artists; Cosimo de' Medici ('the Elder') and his grandson Lorenzo ('the Magnificent') were unofficial rulers of Florence.
extra: They patronised Ghiberti, Donatello, Botticelli, Michelangelo and the young Machiavelli.

back: The Florentine poet who wrote the Divine Comedy in the Tuscan vernacular, making it the literary language of Italy; he was exiled after a political dispute in 1302.
extra: His work shows the transition from the medieval to the early-modern world view.

back: Often called the 'father of the Italian Renaissance' for his revival of classical learning and his sonnets to Laura; his correspondence with Boccaccio helped to define the humanist program.
extra: He climbed Mt Ventoux in 1336 and was the first to write about mountaineering as a spiritual experience.

back: The Florentine painter of the Primavera and The Birth of Venus, the most celebrated images of the mythological Renaissance; his early work was more naturalistic and religious.
extra: He later turned to severe religious art after the influence of Savonarola.

back: The polymath of the High Renaissance: painter (Mona Lisa, The Last Supper), anatomist, engineer, architect and inventor; he never married and was employed by the Duke of Milan and by the French king.
extra: His notebooks contain thousands of drawings of anatomy, optics, hydraulics and flying machines.

back: The Florentine painter, sculptor and architect who painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508-1512) and the Last Judgment (1536-1541), and sculpted the David and the Pieta.
extra: He also designed the dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome.

back: The greatest dramatist of the English Renaissance, born in Stratford-upon-Avon; he wrote or co-wrote 38 plays and 154 sonnets in his career.
extra: He was an actor and shareholder in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, the playhouse company of the Globe in London.

back: Shakespeare's tragedy of the young Danish prince who is commanded by his father's ghost to avenge his murder; it became the most performed and imitated play in the Western theatre.
extra: It contains the soliloquies 'To be or not to be' and 'What a piece of work is a man'.

back: Shakespeare's sequence of 154 sonnets, published by the printer Thomas Thorpe, addressed to a 'Fair Youth' and a 'Dark Lady' and exploring love, beauty, time and death.
extra: It was the first major English sonnet sequence to use the Shakespearean rhyme scheme (ABAB CDCD EE).

back: The German of Mainz who developed the movable-type printing press around 1440; his 42-line Bible (c. 1455) was the first major book printed in Europe.
extra: Printing spread literacy, cheapened books, and was a key factor in the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

back: The Florentine diplomat and author of 'The Prince' (1532) and 'Discourses on Livy', the foundations of modern political science and realpolitik.
extra: He was tortured and imprisoned by the Medici after a failed coup, and wrote The Prince in exile.

back: The Dutch humanist of Bruges, called 'the prince of the humanists', who wrote in Latin across Europe and satirised the church in 'In Praise of Folly' (1511).
extra: He refused to take sides in the Reformation and remained a Catholic to the end, though his works were used by both sides.

back: The Swiss-German physician of Basel and Augsburg who revolutionised medicine by introducing chemistry (the 'iatrochemistry') into therapeutics and arguing that dose makes the poison.
extra: He famously burned the works of Galen and Avicenna and was one of the most controversial figures of the sixteenth century.

back: The English explorer and courtier of Elizabeth I who explored the American south-east, planted a short-lived colony at Roanoke, and was executed by James I in 1618.
extra: He is also credited with introducing the potato and tobacco to England, and with the line 'I have not had so much as time to drink my blood' (apocryphal) at his execution.

back: In 1517 the German Augustinian friar Martin Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences, sparking the split of Western Christianity and the birth of Protestantism.
extra: The Reformation spread through Germany, Scandinavia, Switzerland and England, and was opposed by the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

back: The German monk and professor who translated the Bible into German, wrote 'On Christian Liberty' and other works, and whose Ninety-five Theses (1517) started the Reformation.
extra: He was excommunicated in 1521 and declared an outlaw at the Diet of Worms, but was protected by his patron, Frederick the Wise of Saxony.

back: Before the German imperial diet Luther refused to recant his writings and was given a safe-conduct to leave; he was then declared a 'villain' and outlaw of the empire.
extra: His friends spirited him to Wartburg castle, where he translated the New Testament into German (1522).

back: The French theologian who reformed Geneva and wrote the 'Institutes of the Christian Religion' (1536), the most systematic statement of Reformed (Calvinist) theology.
extra: Calvinism spread to Scotland (Presbyterianism), the Netherlands, and to New England, where it shaped the culture of the Puritans.

back: English reformers who sought to 'purify' the Church of England of Roman Catholic practices; they emigrated to New England in the 17th century and founded the Massachusetts Bay Colony (1630).
extra: Their theology and discipline shaped the early culture of the American colonies.

back: The Catholic reform council that reaffirmed core Catholic doctrines, reformed abuses, and reasserted the authority of the Pope and the church; it is the defining moment of the Counter-Reformation.
extra: Its decrees on the sacraments, the Bible and the Mass remain the foundation of Catholic teaching.

back: The Spanish soldier turned priest who founded the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) in 1540 and wrote the 'Spiritual Exercises', the manual of Catholic spiritual direction.
extra: The Jesuits became the main force of the Counter-Reformation, running schools and missions across Europe and the world.

back: The Polish cleric whose 'De Revolutionibus' (1543) placed the Sun at the centre of the planetary system, overturning the Ptolemaic-Earth-centred model that had dominated since antiquity.
extra: The heliocentric model was a key step of the Scientific Revolution and the beginning of modern astronomy.

back: The Italian astronomer who used the telescope to discover the moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus, and sunspots, providing the observational evidence for the Copernican system.
extra: He was tried and convicted by the Roman Inquisition in 1633 for 'vehement suspicion of heresy' and spent his last years under house arrest.

back: The German astronomer who discovered the three laws of planetary motion, including that planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus, providing the mathematical basis for Newton's later theory of gravity.
extra: His 'Astronomia Nova' (1609) was the first rigorous treatment of planetary motion.

back: The English mathematician and physicist who formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation in 'Principia Mathematica' (1687) and independently invented the calculus.
extra: He also studied optics, showing that white light is a mixture of the colours of the spectrum.

back: The English 'father of chemistry' whose experimental work ('The Sceptical Chymist', 1661) distinguished true chemical elements from the alchemical 'principles' and defined a chemical theory on experimental grounds.
extra: He also formulated Boyle's law (the inverse relation of pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature).

back: The French mathematician and philosopher of La Rochelle and Amsterdam who formulated the method of rational doubt and the formula 'I think, therefore I am' (Cogito ergo sum).
extra: He was the first to describe the method of analytic geometry (the Cartesian coordinate system).

back: The American polymath who demonstrated the nature of electricity with the kite experiment (1752), invented the lightning rod, bifocal glasses, and the Franklin stove, and was a key figure in American independence.
extra: He was a signer of both the Declaration of Independence (1776) and the US Constitution (1787), and served as ambassador to France.

back: The Swedish botanist who invented the binomial system of naming species (genus and species) in 'Systema Naturae' (1735) and 'Species Plantarum' (1753), still the standard of biological nomenclature.
extra: He classified plants by the number of their stamens and was knighted in 1761.

back: The French naturalist who, in 1809, proposed the first complete theory of evolution by the inheritance of acquired characteristics (the giraffe's long neck), before Darwin's theory of natural selection.
extra: His ideas were later discredited but he was an important early evolutionary thinker.

back: The English naturalist who, on the basis of his voyage on the 'Beagle' (1831-1836) and of 20 years of study, published 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859, presenting the theory of evolution by natural selection.
extra: The work caused a major scientific and theological controversy in Victorian Britain.

front: The First World War ended with an armistice on {{c1::11 November 1918}} in Compiegne.
extra: Armistice was signed in a railway carriage.

front: The largest Nazi concentration camp of the Holocaust was {{c1::Auschwitz}}.
extra: Located in occupied Poland.

front: During the Holocaust, approximately {{c1::six million}} European Jews were murdered.
extra: Represented about two-thirds of European Jewish population.

front: Churchill warned that an {{c1::iron curtain}} had descended across Europe in 1946.
extra: Speech given in Fulton, Missouri.

front: The Berlin Wall was erected by East Germany on {{c1::13 August 1961}}.
extra: Divided the city until 1989.

front: Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union until his death in {{c1::1953}}.
extra: Led USSR through WWII and onset of Cold War.

front: The Soviet Union was officially dissolved on {{c1::25 December 1991}}.
extra: Marked the end of the Cold War.

front: The US Declaration of Independence was adopted on {{c1::4 July 1776}}.
extra: Adopted in Philadelphia.

front: The United States Constitution was signed on {{c1::17 September 1787}} in Philadelphia.
extra: Replaced Articles of Confederation.

front: The storming of the {{c1::Bastille}} on 14 July 1789 marked the start of the French Revolution.
extra: Celebrated as French national holiday.

front: The Declaration of the Rights of Man was adopted in France in {{c1::1789}}.
extra: Foundational human rights document.

front: The Reign of Terror in France ended with the fall of {{c1::Robespierre}} in 1794.
extra: Led the Committee of Public Safety.

front: The heliocentric model of the solar system was published by {{c1::Copernicus}} in 1543.
extra: Published in De revolutionibus orbium coelestium.

front: The first Roman expeditions to Britain were led by {{c1::Julius Caesar}} in 55-54 BC.
extra: Formal conquest came later under Claudius.

front: Julius Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March in {{c1::44 BC}}.
extra: Assassinated in the Roman Senate.

front: Alexander the Great became king of Macedon in {{c1::336 BC}} after Philip II.
extra: Went on to conquer Persian Empire.

front: Alexander the Great died in Babylon in {{c1::323 BC}} at age thirty-two.
extra: Empire subsequently divided among his generals.

front: The ancient Library of Alexandria was founded around {{c1::295 BC}} in Egypt.
extra: Major center of scholarship in ancient world.

front: Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire in {{c1::1453}}, ending Byzantium.
extra: Conquered by Sultan Mehmed II.

front: The Islamic Golden Age began with the Abbasid Caliphate around {{c1::750 AD}}.
extra: Center of learning in Baghdad.

front: The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in {{c1::1099}} after a three-week siege.
extra: Established Crusader states in the Levant.

front: The Third Crusade ended with a truce between Richard I and {{c1::Saladin}} in 1192.
extra: Allowed unarmed Christian pilgrims to visit Jerusalem.

front: The Black Death pandemic arrived in Europe in {{c1::1347}}, killing millions.
extra: Caused by Yersinia pestis plague.

front: King John of England granted the Magna Carta at Runnymede in {{c1::1215}}.
extra: Foundational charter of legal rights.

front: The principal author of the 1776 Declaration of Independence was {{c1::Thomas Jefferson}}.
extra: Adopted by the Continental Congress.

front: The first electric battery, the voltaic pile, was invented by {{c1::Alessandro Volta}} in 1800.
extra: Enabled continuous electric current.
